rows.subtype: Approach: auditing the weekly timetable [Thinking]
rows.description: A student in Class 11 adds up school, three coaching batches, travel and homework, finds 62 hours a week and no rest, and sees that the problem is total load and not lack of effort.

rows.subtype: Approach: prioritising the classes that add most [Action]
rows.description: The student compares which batches clarify concepts versus repeat school content, keeps the two that help most, and uses the freed time for self-study and sleep.

rows.subtype: Approach: attending everything out of fear of falling behind [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student stays in all batches because peers do. Constant sitting leaves no time to absorb the material, and marks stay flat despite exhausting days.

rows.subtype: Approach: adding rest and exercise as fixed items [Revision]
rows.description: After noticing exhaustion, the student blocks a 30-minute walk and a free Sunday afternoon in the calendar, treating rest as a scheduled part of study rather than a reward.

rows.subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
rows.subtype: Approach: choosing one course and finishing it [Action]
rows.description: A student picks a single beginner Python course, sets a goal of one lesson a day, and resists starting other courses until it is completed and a small program of his own is written.

rows.subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
rows.subtype: Approach: joining a study group for accountability [Action]
rows.description: A student teams with two classmates to solve one problem a week, present solutions to each other every Friday, and nudge whoever has skipped, which keeps all three going through dull weeks.

rows.subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
rows.subtype: Approach: tutorial hopping without practice [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student watches video after video, feels he is learning, but when given a blank editor cannot write even a loop because he only ever followed along and never typed his own code.

rows.subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
rows.subtype: Approach: reviewing progress and changing method [Revision]
rows.description: After noticing three weeks without new skills, a student reviews what he did, sees he only watched videos, and switches to solving small exercises first and using videos only when stuck.

rows.subtopic: A marriage disagreement over careers or location
rows.subtype: Approach: writing down each partner's priorities separately [Thinking]
rows.description: A couple facing a job offer in another city each lists what matters most: career growth, closeness to family and finances. Seeing the lists reveals shared values beneath the disagreement.

rows.subtopic: A marriage disagreement over careers or location
rows.subtype: Approach: exploring the options as a joint decision matrix [Thinking]
rows.description: They score staying, moving, or a trial year against agreed criteria and weights. The score is not final, but it turns an emotional argument into an organised discussion.

rows.subtopic: A marriage disagreement over careers or location
rows.subtype: Approach: winning the argument through pressure [Pitfall]
rows.description: One partner repeats reasons more forcefully and uses guilt. The other gives in, but resentment lingers and reappears months later in unrelated fights.

rows.subtopic: A marriage disagreement over careers or location
rows.subtype: Approach: revisiting the decision after the trial period [Revision]
rows.description: At the six month review they note what improved and what hurt, such as long weekends apart. They adjust by adding a shorter commute and a visit schedule rather than reversing everything.

rows.subtype: Approach: dividing the price by weekly pocket money [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy wants a Rs 600 remote-control car and gets Rs 50 a week. He divides and works out twelve weeks, and decides to keep going because the number seems reachable.

rows.subtype: Approach: earning extra by doing jobs at home [Action]
rows.description: A boy asks his parents whether he can earn Rs 10 for washing the family car on Sundays. The extra income shortens his wait from twelve weeks to eight.

rows.subtype: Approach: spending on snacks and forgetting the goal [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child gets money each week but buys chips and stickers at the shop near school. After a month the jar is nearly empty because small spends were never counted.

rows.subtype: Approach: setting a smaller first target [Revision]
rows.description: Noticing he feels discouraged, the boy sets a first goal of Rs 200 and celebrates when he reaches it. Smaller steps rebuild his patience and he carries on toward the full price.

rows.subtype: Approach: choosing the right moment and mood [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy wants permission for a sleepover and waits until his father has relaxed after dinner, rather than asking when he is tired or on a call.

rows.subtype: Approach: preparing reasons and answers to objections [Action]
rows.description: Before asking for a bicycle, a girl lists why she needs it, how she will be safe, and what she will do to earn part of the cost, so she is ready for questions.

rows.subtype: Approach: nagging and repeating the demand [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child asks for a mobile phone every day and cries when refused, and the parents become firmer, because pressure without reasons builds resistance.

rows.subtype: Approach: accepting a no and asking what would change it [Revision]
rows.description: Told no to a late outing, a boy calmly asks what he would need to show, and the parents say trust with earlier smaller outings, giving him a clear step to work toward.

rows.subtype: Approach: trial and error [Action]
rows.description: A child stacks wooden blocks into a tower, watches it fall at the sixth block, and simply builds it again with the blocks in a slightly different order.

rows.subtype: Approach: simple step list [Thinking]
rows.description: A child tells herself, "First the big blocks, then the small ones, then the flag on top," and builds in that order. The list keeps the tower's shape in mind as it grows.

rows.subtype: Approach: magical thinking [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child says "stay up" to the tower and insists the red block is lucky, so it goes on top. When the tower wobbles anyway, the child blames the block rather than the narrow base.

rows.subtype: Approach: if-then rule [Revision]
rows.description: After three collapses a child decides, "If it wobbles, make the bottom wider," and uses the rule on the next tower. A tested rule replaces the guess.
